Sorting sides as a ≤ b ≤ c with entries from 1 through 4, the strict triangle inequality yields 13 triples: 111, 122, 133, 144, 222, 223, 233, 234, 244, 333, 334, 344, 444. The four equilateral triples form one similarity class, and 122 and 244 form another. There are no other proportional pairs, leaving 13 − 3 − 1 = 9 classes. At most one triangle can be selected from each class, and choosing one from each attains nine. SSS justifies representing congruence classes by sorted side triples.

routes.label: Inradius and the half-angle at B

audits.mathematicalReason: The incenter has semiperimeter s = 39 and triangle area √(39·12·13·14) = 78√14, so the inradius is r = 2√14. The cosine law gives cos B = 113/225, hence sin(B/2) = 2√14/15, taking the positive root because B/2 is acute. Thus BI = r/sin(B/2) = 15. The second route is independently valid: if D is the intersection of the B-angle bisector with AC, then AD = 27/2 and DC = 25/2. Stewart gives BD = 45/2. Applying the angle-bisector theorem to AI in triangle ABD gives BI/ID = AB/AD = 2, so BI = (2/3)BD = 15.

Let pᵢ be the escape probability from pad i. The current pad retains all information needed for future transitions. The boundary values are p₀ = 0 and p₁₀ = 1, and first-step conditioning gives 10pᵢ = i pᵢ₋₁ + (10−i)pᵢ₊₁. Setting dᵢ = pᵢ−pᵢ₋₁ gives dᵢ₊₁ = i dᵢ/(10−i), so dₖ = d₁/C(9,k−1). Consequently 1 = d₁ Σⱼ₌₀⁹ 1/C(9,j) = d₁·146/63. Since p₁ = d₁, the answer is 63/146. Absorption occurs almost surely because from every interior state there is a uniformly positive probability of reaching a boundary within a bounded number of jumps.

For proposed bases u < v and legs p,q, feasibility requires that p,q,v−u form a nondegenerate triangle. Of the six base pairs, only (3,11), (5,11), and (7,11) satisfy this condition. Their auxiliary triangles have sides (5,7,8), (3,7,6), and (3,5,4), giving trapezoid areas (35/2)√3, (32/3)√5, and 27. The radicands 3 and 5 are squarefree. Therefore the requested sum is 35/2 + 32/3 + 27 + 3 + 5 = 379/6, whose floor is 63. Both height routes are valid; horizontal projections must be allowed to be signed, since a valid trapezoid can overhang a base endpoint.

routes.label: Equal chords and the cosine law

audits.mathematicalReason: Write OX = OY = r. Since Z is exterior to C₁, r < OZ = 11. On C₂, the equal chords OX and OY imply that angles OZX and OZY are equal or supplementary. Their cosine-law expressions are (290−r²)/286 and (170−r²)/154. Both are positive when r < 11, so the angles are acute and must be equal. Equating the expressions gives 154(290−r²) = 286(170−r²), hence r² = 30. The supplementary branch would instead give r² = 212 and is excluded by exteriority. The Ptolemy route is also valid: O and Z lie on opposite arcs determined by X,Y, so the cyclic ordering gives 11·XY = 20r; combining this with supplementary opposite angles and the cosine law again gives r² = 30.

In the usual shadow-measurement model, the vertical objects and parallel sunlight form similar right triangles on level ground. If h is the tree height, h/6 = 2/1.5, so h = 8 m. Establishing and using this measurement proportion directly matches the practical similar-triangle scope.

Being inside or on the circle means (x−5)² + (−x−5)² ≤ 100. This simplifies to 2x² + 50 ≤ 100, or −5 ≤ x ≤ 5. Including both endpoints gives eleven integers. The geometric route is also valid: the perpendicular foot from (5,5) to y = −x is the origin, its distance is 5√2, and the half-chord length is 5√2. Since the distance from the origin to (x,−x) is |x|√2, the same coordinate bounds follow.

Let the initial population be a². The middle condition gives a² + 150 = b² + 9, so (b−a)(b+a) = 141. The positive factor pairs (1,141) and (3,47) give a = 70 or a = 22. The final condition excludes 70 because 70² + 300 = 5200 is not square, while 22² + 300 = 784 = 28². Thus the initial population was 484, and the twenty-year growth was (300/484)·100% ≈ 61.98%, closest to 62%. The integer-square constraints and the original-population denominator are both correctly represented by the candidate scopes.
